note: First-run results are recorded history. “Now” values are read from the latest result files each time this page loads.

items.title: Finding the right laptop
items.question: If you type a laptop name, do we find the right one (and not a wrong one)?
items.first_note: It treated “laptop bag” as a laptop.
items.meaning: Specific model names, ambiguous families, unknown laptops and typos were all handled; accessories are now recognised.

items.title: Safety checks on web pages and quotes
items.question: Can a link or a page trick the app into reading private addresses, and can an invented quote slip in?
items.first: Blocked 23 of 23 unsafe addresses; got 28 of 28 link rules right; rejected 39 of 39 altered quotes
items.meaning: The guards that decide what we may read, and whether a quote is word-for-word real, held up in every test.

items.title: Spotting hidden instructions in reviews (pattern filter)
items.question: Do we catch text that tries to give orders to the software?
items.first: Caught 1 of 20 attacks we had not seen; 3 of 20 harmless sentences wrongly flagged
items.first_note: After tuning it caught 20 of 20 on the examples it was tuned on, which proves nothing.
items.meaning: A pattern filter cannot recognise new wording. We do not rely on it alone.

items.title: What a hidden instruction can actually do
items.question: If someone plants an instruction in a review, can it change what you see?
items.first: 3 of 20 unseen attacks slipped through as one fake positive claim
items.first_note: The model flagged 4, and 12 produced nothing.
items.meaning: The damage is limited: one fake claim counts as one owner, a Serious Problem needs two, the report text is written by rules, and every claim must be an exact quote.

items.title: Checking claims (battery, RAM, weight, price…)
items.question: Does the Claim Checker reach the verdict a careful person would?
items.first: First run on new claims: 26 of 35, then 19 of 41
items.first_note: Both sets were then used to fix the engine, so the “now” score is not a fair test.
items.meaning: It handled the common cases, but each fresh set exposed new gaps. Expect more until a person checks it.

items.title: Reading owner reviews
items.question: When the software reads a review, does it pull out the right topics and opinions?
items.first: Right topic found about 66% of the time (precision) and 69% of the topics found (recall); opinion right on 46 of 55
items.first_note: Measured on 40 fresh reviews, before looking at results.
items.meaning: Good enough to show what owners say, not good enough to treat a single finding as certain. That is why every finding opens the original review.

items.title: Finding the relevant reviews
items.question: Does search pull up the reviews that are actually about your topic?
items.first: Keyword search alone 0.52, meaning-based 0.63, both together 0.64 (scale 0 to 1)
items.meaning: Using both kinds of search beat keywords alone.

items.title: Looking up a laptop we don’t have
items.question: When we read a maker’s page, are the facts we keep correct?
items.first: 8 of 8 kept facts correct, but only 2 of 5 new laptops gave any usable facts
items.first_note: Many maker pages are blocked, rate-limited or need a browser to display.
items.meaning: What we show is accurate, but we often show little. Looked-up laptops never have owner reviews.

items.title: Understanding what you type
items.question: When you describe your needs in your own words, do we get the use, budget and brands to avoid right?
items.first: What you'll use it for: 21 of 24 right. Budget: 24 of 24. Brands to avoid: 24 of 24
items.first_note: 24 fresh requests including Hinglish. Missed: 'edit videos for YouTube', 'streaming', 'travel for work'. Priority words were all found, but I wrote the test knowing the word list, so treat that as optimistic.
items.meaning: Reliable for ordinary phrasing. Unusual wording can be missed, which is why the page shows what we understood and lets you correct it.

items.title: Rating each topic from reviews
items.question: When the fast reader labels a review (battery, screen…), is the label right, and does it find the topics owners mention?
items.first: Reader 1: right 89% of the time when it labelled but found only 46% of topics. Reader 2 (fresh reviews): precision 81%, finds 95%, happy/unhappy right 68 of 72. Reader 3, the one in use, 4 times faster (fresh reviews): precision 88%, finds 83%, happy/unhappy right 58 of 65
items.first_note: Each reader was tested on reviews labelled before the test was run, once. Labels were written by Claude, not a person.
items.meaning: Ratings now cover most of what owners say. About 1 in 8 happy/unhappy calls is wrong, so a single rating can be off; many owners per rating average that out, which is why each rating shows how many owners it rests on.

items.title: Checking a pasted listing (Listing Lie Detector)
items.question: Given a laptop listing, are the verdicts on each claim right, and is the right laptop matched?
items.first: First run on 24 listings: 46 of 68 verdicts right (68%); right laptop for only 17 of 24
items.first_note: It matched a 2024 M3 MacBook to our 2020 M1, matched US Dell and Acer listings to US laptops, and called Apple's published 18-hour claim 'very unlikely'. Fresh sets afterwards: 29 of 32 right (91%), then 23 of 23 (100%, but the set was easy and one Hinglish sentence got a verdict on half its meaning). The answer keys were written by the same AI that wrote the code, from real published specs retyped into listing style; no person has checked them.
items.meaning: Good on the clear cases it was tested on. Treat it as promising, not proven: small sets, one author, no real seller listings yet.
